September 21, 2026


Debbie-Anne A. Reese, Secretary
Federal Energy Regulatory Commission
888 First Street, N.E.
Washington, D.C. 20426

Re:     Texas Gas Transmission, LLC
        Dearborn County Lateral Project
        Docket No. CP26-536-000
        Response to Environmental Information Request

Dear Ms. Reese:

          Texas Gas Transmission, LLC (“Texas Gas”) hereby submit for filing with the Federal Energy
Regulatory Commission (“Commission”) its response to the Commission’s Environmental Information Request
issued on September 15, 2026 (“Data Request”). Pursuant to the provision of the Commission’s Rules of
Practice and Procedure, 18 C.F.R. §385.2010, a copy is being served to each person whose name appears on the
official service list for this proceeding.

        The undersigned is the authorized representative and should be considered the respondent to the Data
Request. If you have any questions or need additional information, please contact me at (713) 321-8420 or at
shannon.miller@bwpipelines.com.


Sincerely,

/s/Shannon Miller.

Shannon Miller
Director, Certificates

Texas Gas Transmission, LLC

         Dearborn County Lateral Project

            Docket No. CP26-536-000

RESPONSE TO THE FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY
     COMMISSION’S INFORMATION REQUEST
             Dated September 15, 2026




                    Volume I

            PUBLIC INFORMATION




                 September 2026
                                  Texas Gas Transmission, LLC
                                  Docket No. CP26-536-000




General Project Information

1. Provide a response to all comments filed on FERC’s docket including those not
   addressed in Texas Gas’ response to comments on August 13, 2026 (Accession Nos.
   20260706-5181, 20260828-5182, 20260828-5094 and 20260911-5250).

Response:

A response to the comment filed under Accession No. 20260706-5181 was included in Texas Gas
Transmission, LLC’s (Texas Gas) July 30, 2026, response to comments. The comment filed under
Accession No. 20260911-5250 is related to Venture Global’s CP2 LNG Expansion Project (Docket
No. CP26-530), and is therefore not applicable to the Dearborn County Lateral Project.

Responses to all other comments filed in Docket No. CP26-536-00 that were not addressed in Texas
Gas’s previously filed responses, are provided as Attachment 1 to this response.




                                             2
                                   Texas Gas Transmission, LLC
                                   Docket No. CP26-536-000



Resource Report 10

2. According to Resource Report 10, the company states that Alternative 1, Alternative 2,
   Alternative 3, and Alternative 5 are not viable due to conflicts with publicly identified
   conservation easements. Please provide a detailed description of each conservation
   easement referenced in Resource Report 10, including:
       a. the specific location and boundary of each easement, clearly shown on a map or
          aerial figure;
       b. the environmental resources protected by each easement (e.g., wetlands, floodplain
          habitat, cultural resources, forests, species, land-use restrictions); and
       c. a route-specific evaluation explaining precisely how each alternative (1, 2, 3, and
          5) would intersect or impact these easements, including construction feasibility
          constraints, regulatory restrictions, landowner permissions, and any other
          environmental or land-use concerns.

   Response:

   a. An overview map that includes the specific location and boundary of each conservation
      easement identified in Resource Report 10 – Alternatives is provided as Attachment 2.

   b. There are three predominant conservation easements identified in Resource Report 10;
      an Oxbow Agricultural Conservation Easement, a Hamilton County Park District
      (HCPD) “Shawnee Lookout” Conservation Easement, and an HCPD Floodplain
      Easement. All three easements were identified with the Protected Areas Database of
      the United States (PAD-US), as managed by U.S. Geological System (USGS). A
      description of all three, including which alternative routes identified in Resource
      Report 10 cross through each and the easement-specific constraints if adopted, are
      provided below.

      i.   The Oxbow Agricultural Conservation Easement (presented in the originally-filed
           Appendix 10A as “Oxbow Conservation Easement”) is a part of Oxbow, Inc.’s
           nature conservancy in Indiana on the floodplain of the Great Miami River at its
           confluence with the Ohio River. Much of this fertile wetland is utilized as
           traditional protected farmland to feed migrating and over-wintering animals and
           function as an edge ecosystem, as well as provide an income to support Oxbow,
           Inc.’s goal in preserving this vital habitat (USGS, 2022; Indiana Land Protection
           Alliance, 2023).

           If adopted, Alternative Routes 1, 2, and 5 would impact this easement directly.
           Alternatives directly intersecting the Oxbow Agricultural Conservation Easement
           temporarily impact agricultural land during construction and remove the food
           sources for the migrating and over-wintering wildlife that depend on its
           agricultural production, both during construction and potentially several planting
           cycles following during intensive restoration activities. Additionally, given the
           farmland’s importance on maintaining the nearby wetland habitat, construction
           through this edge ecosystem could affect the drainage and nearby contours of the
                                              3
                               Texas Gas Transmission, LLC
                               Docket No. CP26-536-000



       Oxbow which would further impact the existing agricultural processes and water
       supply systems in place. Should any of these alternatives be adopted, permission
       would need to be obtained through coordination with Oxbow, Inc.as it manages the
       conservation easement on its owned land. Oxbow, Inc.’s primary mission is
       conservation and preliminary discussions regarding survey permission on their
       property for this project was denied. As stated in Resource Report 10, construction
       of new infrastructure within the easement area would be subject to individually-
       negotiated and potentially restrictive terms. Due to these environmental impacts
       and potential changes to necessary habitat, selecting an alternative route that
       would impact the Oxbow Agricultural Conservation Easement would result in
       greater impact than the proposed route.

ii.    The HCPD “Shawnee Lookout” Conservation Easement (presented in the
       originally-filed Appendix 10A as “HCPD Conservation Easements”) is located in
       Ohio adjacent to Shawnee Lookout, a historic park at the confluence of the Great
       Miami River and the Ohio. The collective conservation easements that the HCPD
       manages for Shawnee Lookout are defined as “recreation or education easements”
       and work to promote environmental education, preserve the area’s scenic value,
       and protect the wetlands in the park to allow space for waterfowl, wading birds,
       and other wildlife throughout the year (USGS, 2022; eBird, 2026).

       If adopted, Alternative Routes 1, 2, 3, and 5 would impact this easement directly.
       Alternatives directly intersecting the Shawnee Lookout Conservation Easement
       would introduce significant constructability concerns, as the easement’s terrain
       varies between low-lying wetlands, mature forest, prairies, and high overlooks on
       ridges (see the Route Alternatives Maps provided in Attachment 2 that include both
       a topographic map and aerial imagery of the landscape impacted by the Project
       alternatives). Similar to the Oxbow Agricultural Conservation Easement, wetlands
       in the area offer vital habitat to nearby wildlife and construction could result in
       disproportionate impacts to the biological stability of the area. Additionally,
       Shawnee Lookout is an important cultural resource, as it houses major
       archeological sites including Woodland-period burial mounds and other
       subsurface features that would need to be maneuvered around. Should any of these
       alternatives be adopted, permission would need to be obtained through
       coordination with the HCPD as it manages the conservation easement on its owned
       land. Due to these environmental impacts, constructability concerns, and potential
       impact to important cultural features, selecting an alternative route that would
       impact the Shawnee Lookout Conservation Easement would result in greater
       impact than the proposed route.

iii.   The HCPD Floodplain Easement (identified in the originally filed Appendix 10A as
       “HCPD”) is administered by the Natural Resources Conservation Service (NRCS)
       under the Emergency Watershed Protection – Floodplain Easement Program. Lands
       enrolled in this program typically have a documented history of repeated flooding, and
       the easement is intended to restore, protect, maintain, and enhance natural floodplain
       functions and associated wildlife habitat (USGS 2022; NRCS 2009).

                                          4
                            Texas Gas Transmission, LLC
                            Docket No. CP26-536-000



If adopted, Alternative Routes 1 and 5 would directly intersect this easement. Routing
through the HCPD Floodplain Easement would introduce significant
construction-phase safety concerns due to the area’s high flood risk. Any alteration of
ground contours in this location could increase drainage and flood-routing impacts
across the broader landscape, including the low-lying agricultural areas near the Ohio
River flood basin that rely on the floodplain’s stability for crop production and wildlife
support.

In addition, unlike the other two conservation easements discussed above—each
managed by the organizations that own the underlying land—the HCPD Floodplain
Easement is regulated by NRCS, and obtaining a pipeline easement within it would
require navigating a more stringent federal review process with strict restoration and
compliance requirements due to the elevated flood-risk profile.

Given the combination of construction safety risks, heightened potential for increased
flooding impacts, and the more restrictive regulatory framework, selecting an
alternative route that intersects the HCPD Floodplain Easement would result in greater
overall environmental and operational impact than the proposed route.

        Accessed September 2026.

Indiana Land Protection Alliance. 2023. Preserving Legacies: Oxbow, Inc’s Wetlands and
         Farmlands Support Migration Crossroads. https://protectindianaland.org/wetlands-at-the-
         crossroads/. Accessed September 2026.

Natural Resources Conservation Service – Ohio. 2009. Questions and answers regarding the
         NRCS floodplain easement option.
         https://cms2.revize.com/revize/hamiltoncountyoh/Documents/Government/Departments/
         Planning%20and%20Development/Stormwater%20and%20Infrastructure/Reports%20an
         d%20Publications/FloodplainEasementOH.pdf. Accessed September 2026.

U.S. Geological Survey. 2022. PAD-US Data Overview. https://www.usgs.gov/programs/gap-
        analysis-project/science/pad-us-data-overview#overview. Accessed September 2026.




                                         5
                                       Texas Gas Transmission, LLC
                                       Docket No. CP26-536-000




   3. Evaluate an alternative route that:
          stays entirely north of the conservation easements;
          crosses into Ohio without entering Kentucky; and
          rejoins the general Alternative 3 et al. corridor southward, or another
              acceptable route, to reach the Miami Fort Power Plant.

       Provide a map showing the conceptual route described above as well as any other newly
developed or considered alternative routes. Discuss and provide a comparison of affected
environmental resources and feasibility constraints between the alternative(s) and the proposed
route.


       Response:

       Texas Gas has evaluated a conceptual route alternative ("Alternative 6") that would avoid
       the identified conservation easements while remaining entirely within Indiana and Ohio.
       Alternative 6 would originate at the existing Texas Gas 26-inch Mainline System (MLS)
       26-1TT and MLS 26-2TT pipelines approximately 6 miles northeast of the proposed Tie-
       In Facility, proceed generally southeast, then turn west-southwest north of the Ohio River
       before terminating at the Miami Fort Power Plant.

       Mapping exhibits depicting the Proposed Route and all major route alternatives,
       including Alternative 6, are provided in Attachment 2 to this Environmental Information
       Request (EIR). Table 1 below compares the environmental and engineering
       characteristics of Alternative 6 with those of the Proposed Route and the other
       alternatives evaluated in Resource Report 10.

                                                                                         8
                                 Texas Gas Transmission, LLC
                                 Docket No. CP26-536-000



Land Disturbance and Corridor Co-Location

Conceptual Alternative 6 is approximately 9.68 miles in length and avoids both the identified
conservation easements and any crossing into Kentucky. Based on the conceptual
evaluation, Alternative 6 would result in approximately 29.68 fewer acres of land
disturbance than the Proposed Route and would provide a slightly greater degree of co-
location with existing utility corridors.

However, conceptual Alternative 6 traverses several areas of steep terrain that would
require extensive grading, side-slope benching, and additional construction workspace. The
temporary workspace required for safe construction, staging, spoil management, and slope
stabilization would substantially reduce, and potentially eliminate, the apparent land
disturbance advantage identified at the conceptual planning level when compared to the
Proposed Route.

Residential and Noise-Sensitive Area Impacts

Alternative 6 would result in greater direct and indirect impacts to nearby residences than
the Proposed Route. After crossing the Whitewater River, the route would continue south
and immediately cross Interstate 275. These crossings would likely require adjacent
horizontal directional drills (HDDs) at the Whitewater River and Interstate 275. The
proposed HDD locations are immediately adjacent to a residential neighborhood containing
more than 200 noise-sensitive areas (NSAs), with additional NSAs located within one-half
mile of the crossing locations. South of Interstate 275, the route would continue through
agricultural land where additional HDDs, or a single longer HDD, would likely be
necessary to cross U.S. Highway 50 and the Great Miami River. These HDD activities would
increase construction duration, noise generation, and potential impacts to nearby residences
relative to the Proposed Route.

Engineering and Constructability Considerations

Conceptual Alternative 6 presents several constructability challenges not associated with
the Proposed Route. The route would require multiple HDD crossings in close succession,
including crossings of Whitewater River, Interstate 275, U.S. Highway 50 and the Great
Miami River. Steep terrain south of these crossings, together with the constraints imposed
by Miamiview Road, would limit available workspace and HDD pull-string areas. As a
result, construction activities would be more complex, require significantly more temporary
workspace, and would involve greater engineering, safety, and logistical challenges than the
Proposed Route.

Impacts to Shawnee Lookout Park

To avoid the identified conservation easements while remaining entirely within Indiana and
Ohio, Alternative 6 would require approximately 1.7 miles of routing through Shawnee
Lookout Park, potentially impacting park resources and visits. As discussed in the response
to EIR Comment No. 2.b, Alternative 6 would avoid the managed recreation and education

                                             9
                                     Texas Gas Transmission, LLC
                                     Docket No. CP26-536-000



  easement associated with Shawnee Lookout Park; however, construction would traverse
  environmentally sensitive resources within Shawnee Lookout Park, including low-lying
  wetlands, mature forest communities, prairie habitats, and ridge-top overlooks.

Although conceptual Alternative 6 minimizes wetland impacts, construction would require
substantial tree clearing on steep slopes and ridgelines. Such clearing could affect drainage
patterns in adjacent wetland systems and would likely necessitate additional temporary
workspace to safely construct the pipeline.

Alternative 6 would also directly affect several hiking trails within Shawnee Lookout Park and
would temporarily disrupt recreational use for an entire summer season during construction.
While efforts were made to maximize co-location with existing corridors, maintenance of a
permanent pipeline right-of-way through forested portions of Shawnee Look Park would
create long-term visual impacts by converting forested areas to maintained utility corridor.
As a result, recreational users will experience a lasting change in the visual character of
portions of Shawnee Lookout Park.

 Cultural Resource Impacts

Shawnee Lookout Park contains significant cultural and archaeological resources, including
Woodland-period burial mounds and other potentially important subsurface features.

Development of Alternative 6 would require extensive cultural resource investigations and
coordination with the Ohio State Historic Preservation Office to identify, evaluate, and avoid
potential impacts to historic properties. Additional evaluation would be necessary to
determine whether complete avoidance of cultural resources could be achieved while
maintaining the route's objective of avoiding the nearby conservation easements.

Coordination would also be required with Great Parks of Hamilton County to address park
management concerns and ensure that public safety, recreational access, and resource
protection objectives are maintained during both construction and operation of the Project.
Hamilton County Parks Department was contacted about securing survey permission for this
Project and consent was not granted.

Conclusion

Based on the analysis presented above, although Alternative 6 is shorter than the Proposed
Route and avoids the identified conservation easements while remaining entirely within Indiana
and Ohio, the route would introduce greater residential, recreational, cultural, visual, and
constructability impacts. The additional impacts associated with Alternative 6 identified in this
response are based solely on Texas Gas's evaluation of publicly available information.
Because this evaluation is limited to available data sources, there may be additional impacts
that Texas Gas was unable to identify or assess.

In addition, the multiple HDD crossings, steep terrain, constrained workspaces, and increased
coordination and future routing modification requirements reduce the overall feasibility of the
                                                10
                                       Texas Gas Transmission, LLC
                                       Docket No. CP26-536-000



alternative. Therefore, based on the comparative evaluation of environmental resources,
engineering constraints, and overall project feasibility, the Commission should conclude that
Alternative 6 is not preferable to the Proposed Route. The Proposed Route remains the most
environmentally sound and technically feasible alternative for meeting the Project's objectives.

                                                                               The Commission should further recognize that, pursuant to Section
                                                                               192.615 of PHMSA’s regulations, Texas Gas will establish an
                                                                               emergency plan that provides written procedures to minimize the
                                                                               hazards from a gas pipeline emergency, including procedures for
                                                                               establishing and maintain liaison with appropriate fire, police, and
                                                                               other public officials to learn the resources and responsibilities of each
                                                                               organization that may respond to a gas pipeline emergency and
                                                                               coordinate mutual assistance in responding to emergencies. Resource
                                                                               Report 11 at 11-6.
